Chapter 8: The Joy and Challenge of Saying Yes to Play
Have you ever noticed how, somewhere along the way, we seem to lose our sense of playfulness? The pressures of being an adult—work, paying bills, taking care of family—can crowd out that spontaneous joy we used to feel as kids. Laughter becomes something rare, almost saved for special occasions or those brief, unexpected moments. But when you start saying “yes” more often, especially during a year of “yes,” something magical happens—the invitation to play starts to show up again.
Maybe it’s as simple as a child asking, “Will you dance with me?” And your first reaction? It’s probably to say no, or just watch from the sidelines. But when you’re committed to saying “yes,” you find yourself stepping onto that dance floor—even if your moves are clumsy and you’re completely off-beat. What happens next is real laughter. The kind that’s unfiltered, honest, and somehow soothing.
Here’s the thing: play isn’t only for kids. It’s actually a way to reconnect with your creativity, curiosity, and those forgotten parts of yourself that you may have pushed aside. It’s about trying something new—maybe it’s picking up a paintbrush for the first time, joining a goofy game, or even just taking a last-minute road trip. What matters isn’t how well you do it, but that you’re willing to let go of feeling self-conscious and just enjoy the moment.
Picture this: a group of friends, gathered for game night. At first, everyone’s a little stiff, not wanting to look silly. But as the night goes on, those walls start to crumble. The room fills with laughter, and for a few hours, nobody’s thinking about deadlines or stress. The worries of the world just melt away. That’s when you realize—play isn’t a distraction from real life. It’s actually a vital part of it.
Saying “yes” to play is a form of self-care. It’s a reminder that joy isn’t something you have to earn by working hard. It’s something you need, just to feel whole. In these lighter moments, you build resilience, strengthen your relationships, and life suddenly feels a little brighter.
So many adults forget how to play, thinking it’s childish or a waste of time. But here’s the truth: play is essential. It sparks creativity, helps us connect with others, and boosts our well-being. When you say “yes” to play, you’re really saying “yes” to life—in all its beautiful mess and unpredictability.
